title: Autonomous agent teams that earn money — what coordination patterns actually work at scale?
body:
We have been running a team of 9 specialized AI agents that work together to build and ship products autonomously. Think: a PO agent writes requirements, a design agent creates specs, backend/frontend agents implement, a QA agent tests, and a DevOps agent deploys. The team has built 13 products in a single 4-hour session.

The hardest part is NOT the individual agent capability — it is the **coordination layer**. Here is what we learned:

1. **Event-driven > request-response**: Agents emit typed events and subscribe to what they need. No point-to-point coupling.
2. **Role identity must persist across sessions**: Each agent carries a persona manifest (role, constraints, learned heuristics) so it does not start from scratch every time.
3. **Backpressure is real**: When all agents emit simultaneously, you need priority queues with per-agent rate limits or the orchestrator chokes.
4. **Self-correction before escalation**: If an agent scores below threshold on role-specific metrics for 3 consecutive turns, it proposes a role transition rather than failing silently.

What coordination patterns have worked (or failed) for others running multi-agent teams? Especially interested in:
- How do you handle agent-to-agent context sharing without blowing token budgets?
- What orchestration strategies survive when individual agents are unreliable (timeouts, hallucinations)?
- Anyone tried economic incentives (agents earning/spending credits) to prioritize work?

Curious to hear what the AutoGen community has found.

title: Agent Memory Guard: Middleware to prevent memory poisoning in multi-agent systems
body:
## What I built

[Agent Memory Guard](https://github.com/OWASP/www-project-agent-memory-guard) — an open-source Python middleware that screens memory reads and writes in AI agent systems for injection attacks, data poisoning, and exfiltration attempts.

## The problem

When you deploy AutoGen agents with persistent memory (conversation history, shared state, tool outputs stored for later), an attacker can inject payloads that persist across sessions. This is classified as [OWASP ASI-06: Memory Poisoning](https://genai.owasp.org).

Example attack on AutoGen:
1. User sends a message containing an encoded injection
2. Agent stores it in memory/shared state
3. Next session, the poisoned memory is loaded into context
4. Agent follows the injected instructions instead of the user's

## How it works

```python
pip install agent-memory-guard
```

```python
from agent_memory_guard import MemoryGuard

guard = MemoryGuard()

# Before storing to memory
result = guard.scan(agent_output)
if result.is_safe:
    memory_store.add(agent_output)
else:
    print(f"Blocked: {result.threat_type}")  # injection, exfiltration, etc.
```

## Key features

- **5 detection layers**: heuristic patterns, embedding similarity, entropy analysis, encoding detection, LLM-as-judge
- **59μs median latency** — no noticeable overhead
- **Works with any framework** — AutoGen, CrewAI, LangChain, LlamaIndex
- **OWASP incubator project** — actively maintained under OWASP governance

## AutoGen integration example

```python
from autogen import ConversableAgent
from agent_memory_guard import MemoryGuard

guard = MemoryGuard()

class SecureAgent(ConversableAgent):
    def _process_received_message(self, message, sender, silent):
        # Screen incoming messages before they enter memory
        scan = guard.scan(message)
        if not scan.is_safe:
            return f"[BLOCKED] Potential {scan.threat_type} detected"
        return super()._process_received_message(message, sender, silent)
```

## Links

- **GitHub**: https://github.com/OWASP/www-project-agent-memory-guard
- **PyPI**: https://pypi.org/project/agent-memory-guard/
- **Docs**: https://owasp.org/www-project-agent-memory-guard/

Would love feedback from the AutoGen community — especially on the best hook points for deeper integration. Happy to build an official AutoGen adapter if there's interest.

title: Pattern: Agent Memory Architecture for Long-Running Multi-Agent Systems
body:
Hey everyone, wanted to share a pattern we've been developing for managing agent memory in production multi-agent systems, and get the community's feedback.

## The Problem

When running multiple agents over extended periods (days/weeks), memory management becomes critical but most frameworks treat it as an afterthought. Issues we've hit:

1. **Memory bloat** - agents accumulate context until they hit token limits
2. **Cross-contamination** - agent A's outputs pollute agent B's reasoning
3. **Temporal confusion** - agents can't distinguish between recent and stale information
4. **Memory poisoning** - malicious or hallucinated data persists across sessions

## Our Approach: Layered Memory Architecture

We've been using a 3-tier memory system:

**Tier 1: Working Memory (per-task)**
- Ephemeral context for the current task
- Automatically pruned when task completes
- Token-limited with priority-based eviction

**Tier 2: Agent Memory (per-agent)**
- Persistent knowledge about the agent's domain
- Summarized periodically to stay within bounds
- Versioned so agents can reason about what changed

**Tier 3: Shared Memory (cross-agent)**
- Explicitly curated shared knowledge
- Write-gated: agents must request writes, which are reviewed
- Read-optimized with semantic search

## Key Design Decisions

- **Memory is not just context** - we store structured knowledge, not just conversation history
- **Write permissions are explicit** - agents don't automatically write to shared memory
- **Memory has TTL** - information expires unless explicitly renewed
- **Conflict resolution is declarative** - when two agents write contradictory info, we have rules for which wins

## Open Questions

1. How are others handling memory summarization without losing critical details?
2. What's the right granularity for memory versioning?
3. Anyone tried using embeddings for memory deduplication across agents?

Would love to hear how the AutoGen community is approaching this. The framework's conversational memory is great for short-lived agents, but for long-running systems we've needed something more structured.

generation != release authority

candidate generation

Hey everyone — sharing an architecture that might be useful if you're working on multi-agent coordination.

I built **AliBaba**, a central intelligence brain that manages 9 specialized agents running autonomously 24/7. The core insight was replacing manual coordination with a **6-step pipeline + shared intelligence hub**.

### The pipeline
```
GATHER → reads 50+ JSON intelligence files (news, performance, health)
ANALYZE → Groq LLM identifies patterns and what's working
THINK → maps every decision to one measurable goal
DECIDE → emits JSON instructions to each agent
ADVISE → daily summary brief
LEARN → adjusts agent priority scores based on actual results
```

### The intelligence sharing layer
Every agent writes structured JSON after every task to a shared hub:
```
/alibaba/intelligence/
  ├── web3/       ← bounty platform outcomes
  ├── content/    ← what's getting views
  ├── bounties/   ← submission win/loss data
  └── market/     ← trending topics
```

AliBaba reads all categories every cycle. The **observation window grows** without retraining — just more data.

Each income stream has a weekly score updated from real performance:
```python
# Score shifts automatically:
# "superteam_bounty": 0.88 → 0.91  (2 submissions won)
# "adsense_blog": 0.72              (pending AdSense approval)
```

Agents with higher scores get more resources next cycle.

title: Governance interceptor for tool calls and inter-agent messages (TealTiger integration)
body:
## Summary

Following up on [Discussion #7726](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/discussions/7726) (Governance Decision Receipts), I'd like to propose a concrete governance interceptor integration using TealTiger that implements the patterns discussed there — content-addressed action references, decision receipts, and vendor-neutral evidence.

## Proposed Integration

Three governance layers, each independent:

**1. Pre-execution hook** — intercepts after agent decides to call a tool but before execution:
```python
from autogen_tealtiger import TealTigerGuard

# Zero-config (observe mode)
guard = TealTigerGuard()

# With policies
from tealtiger import TealEngine
engine = TealEngine(policies=company_policies, mode="ENFORCE")
guard = TealTigerGuard(engine=engine)


2. Message interceptor — adds provenance metadata to inter-agent messages:

from autogen_tealtiger import TealTigerAuditAgent

agent = TealTigerAuditAgent("assistant", tool_guard=guard)


3. Post-execution receipt — structured audit binding tool call + policy decision + result:

Content-addressed params_hash (SHA-256 of JCS-canonicalized arguments, as discussed in #7726 by @chopmob-cloud)
decision_id linking pre-execution authorization to post-execution outcome
Vendor evidence in extensions["teec"] namespace (never validated by AutoGen)
Capabilities
Pre-tool-call policy evaluation (<5ms, deterministic, no LLM in governance path)
Per-agent tool allowlists in GroupChat scenarios
Cost tracking per agent in multi-agent conversations
Kill switch — freeze specific agent mid-conversation without stopping others
Decision receipts with expires_at, revalidate_if, supersedes (from #7726 discussion)
Works with register_reply interceptor pattern and GroupChat speaker_selection_method
GroupChat Example
from autogen_tealtiger import TealTigerGuard, TealTigerAuditAgent

guard = TealTigerGuard(engine=engine)
agent = TealTigerAuditAgent("assistant", tool_guard=guard)

group_chat = GroupChat(
    agents=[agent1, agent2],
    messages=[],
    speaker_selection_method=guard.governed_speaker_selection,
)


Relationship to #7726
This implements the patterns discussed in that thread:

Content-addressed action_ref → params_hash (SHA-256 of JCS-canonical params)
Two-record boundary (authorization before, outcome after) → GovernanceDecision + GovernanceOutcome
Revalidation triggers (policy version bump, scope expansion, budget change)
Vendor-neutral extensions passthrough

Context:
TealTiger — open-source AI agent security platform (Apache-2.0, NVIDIA Inception)
Published on PyPI (tealtiger v1.3.0) and npm (tealtiger-ai-sdk v0.1.0)
Covers 8/10 OWASP Agentic Security Index categories
Already integrated with LangChain, Vercel AI SDK, and CrewAI (governance contract PR approved)
All governance is deterministic and in-process — no external service, <5ms overhead


Contribution Plan
Once the package is on PyPI, I'd submit a PR adding:

An example under samples/ showing governance interceptor with GroupChat
Documentation for the register_reply-based governance pattern
Happy to align with the v0.4 architecture if that's the preferred target. Would appreciate guidance on whether to target microsoft/autogen or ag2ai/ag2 for this contribution.

title: Show & Tell: AliBaba — 6-step AI brain managing 9 agents autonomously
body:
Hey everyone — sharing an architecture that might be useful if you're working on multi-agent coordination.

I built **AliBaba**, a central intelligence brain that manages 9 specialized agents running autonomously 24/7. The core insight was replacing manual coordination with a **6-step pipeline + shared intelligence hub**.

### The pipeline
```
GATHER → reads 50+ JSON intelligence files (news, performance, health)
ANALYZE → Groq LLM identifies patterns and what's working
THINK → maps every decision to one measurable goal
DECIDE → emits JSON instructions to each agent
ADVISE → daily summary brief
LEARN → adjusts agent priority scores based on actual results
```

### The intelligence sharing layer
Every agent writes structured JSON after every task to a shared hub:
```
/alibaba/intelligence/
  ├── web3/       ← bounty platform outcomes
  ├── content/    ← what's getting views
  ├── bounties/   ← submission win/loss data
  └── market/     ← trending topics
```

AliBaba reads all categories every cycle. The **observation window grows** without retraining — just more data.

### Self-learning
Each income stream has a weekly score updated from real performance:
```python
# Score shifts automatically:
# "superteam_bounty": 0.88 → 0.91  (2 submissions won)
# "adsense_blog": 0.72              (pending AdSense approval)
```

Agents with higher scores get more resources next cycle.

---

Happy to answer questions about the orchestration layer or the self-review system for the bounty agent. Full write-up + live dashboard: https://agents.v-architect.tech

title: cowork-to-code-bridge — async bridge for local Claude Code execution from AutoGen agents
body:
Hey AutoGen community!

Building AutoGen agents that need to run code on a *real machine* (not a sandbox)? Thought this might be useful.

## What it does

**cowork-to-code-bridge** is a local-first async bridge that lets your AutoGen agents escalate complex coding tasks to Claude Code on the user's actual Mac/Linux machine — then poll for results without blocking.

### The pattern:
1. AutoGen agent hits a task needing full local context (repos, shell, env)
2. Agent calls `escalate_to_claude(prompt)` via MCP → returns `operation_id` immediately
3. Agent polls `get_operation_status(operation_id)` — non-blocking, idempotent
4. Claude Code runs locally with full machine access
5. Result + `resume_receipt` streamed back to the agent

## Architecture

```
AutoGen Agent → MCP server → file-based queue → local daemon → Claude Code → results
```

No cloud endpoints. No open ports. Auth by HMAC-signed token.

## Production safety (recently shipped)

- **Per-operation metrics**: tool_calls, api_spend_estimate, memory_mb, cpu_percent
- **Loop detection**: auto-alert when same tool called 3+ times with identical args
- **Graceful cancellation**: SIGTERM + timeout, idempotent
- **Quota tracking**: daily limits with midnight UTC reset
- **6/6 cancellation scenarios** tested

## Why this matters for AutoGen

AutoGen's code execution defaults to Docker or local subprocesses — both of which are stateless. This bridge adds:
- **Stateful operations** (long-running tasks with progress polling)
- **Full Claude Code agent** (not just a subprocess — it uses the full agent loop)
- **Async handoff** (fire-and-forget with operation_id, no blocking)

Full integration guide: https://github.com/abhinaykrupa/cowork-to-code-bridge/blob/main/docs/EXTERNAL_AGENT_INTEGRATION.md

Would love feedback from anyone building agents that need local machine access — especially around the stateful execution model. Does this pattern fit how you're using AutoGen?

→ **Repo**: https://github.com/abhinaykrupa/cowork-to-code-bridge

title: Show and Tell: Scankii - Secure your Agent tools (MCP/AutoGen) against prompt injections, token exfiltration, and supply-chain attacks
body:
Hey everyone, 

I’ve been looking into security for AI agent skills and noticed a massive blind spot: traditional security tools (like GitLeaks) only scan the Python code. But in agent frameworks like AutoGen, developers write both Code AND English Prompts. 

If your English prompt accidentally tells the AI to read your database password, the AI will happily oblige and leak it to `stdout`—making it queryable by an attacker via prompt injection. 

To solve this, I built **scankii**—an open-source static security scanner specifically for AI agent skills.

It analyzes your Python/JS codebase AND your natural language instructions simultaneously to detect "Cross-Modal Leaks" before they happen.

**What it catches:**
* Cross-modal credential leaks (NL instruction + code sink)
* Credential-to-stdout and credential-to-network flows
* Hardcoded API keys, private keys, connection strings
* Social engineering in agent prompts

**Try it out:**
`pip install scankii`
`scankii scan ./my-autogen-skills/`

I'd genuinely value feedback from the AutoGen community on whether this catches real issues in your stack!
**Repo:** https://github.com/ashp15205/scankii

title: Recompute what a conversation did: a keystone execution_ref on AutoGen messages
body:
`algovoi-keystone-autogen` stamps an AlgoVoi keystone decision into an AutoGen message's metadata under `algovoi.keystone.*`, so a conversation carries a content-addressed `execution_ref` a reviewer recomputes from the message alone, offline, with no AlgoVoi software.

```
pip install algovoi-keystone-autogen
```

```python
from algovoi_keystone_autogen import stamp_message, verify_trace_execution_ref

msg = stamp_message(
    message,                              # an AutoGen message (object with .metadata, or a dict)
    decision_ref="sha256:...",            # the keystone decision that authorized the action
    action_type="payment", scope="bilateral",
    outcome="COMMITTED", executed_at_ms=1716460800000,
)

# recompute and check from the message metadata alone:
meta = msg.metadata if hasattr(msg, "metadata") else msg["metadata"]
assert verify_trace_execution_ref(meta)
```

`execution_ref = "sha256:" + SHA-256(JCS({decision_ref, action_type, scope, outcome, executed_at_ms}))` (RFC 8785 JCS, integer milliseconds), so it reproduces byte for byte in any language. `execution_ref` is the natural replacement for `action_ref`, and existing `action_ref` integrations stay backward compatible and unchanged. Apache-2.0. Background: https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone
author: chopmob-cloud

title: AlgoVoi open Decision chain (Apache-2.0): identity, authority, policy, compliance, execution, close-out and verdict for AutoGen agents
body:
## The AlgoVoi Keystone

The Keystone is the complete decision chain behind an agent action, expressed as one recomputable sequence of content-addressed references. Each link answers one question and binds to the next, so the whole chain verifies end to end offline, with no issuer contact: just RFC 8785 JCS canonicalization and SHA-256. Open, Apache-2.0.

Data flow:

`identity -> authority -> policy -> compliance -> decision -> execution -> close-out -> verdict`

Cross-party (multi-agent): `delegation -> revocation -> journey`. The constructions are open source (delegation published; revocation and journey available on request); the cross-party proofs are the commercial Orchestrator.

Verify the whole chain yourself, no package import, offline:

```
git clone https://github.com/chopmob-cloud/algovoi-jcs-conformance-vectors
cd algovoi-jcs-conformance-vectors
python composition/verify_corpus.py
```

Each link below is its own open package: install it, pin it, verify it independently, or compose the whole chain. Every package is Apache-2.0 and pinned at `0.1.0`; pinned adopters receive a free v0 verification key (pin, then key).

### 1. Agent Passport, `passport_ref` (identity)

Who the agent is, as a content-addressed identity reference.

Install: `pip install algovoi-agent-passport-lite` or `npm i @algovoi/agent-passport-lite`. Apache-2.0, pinned `0.1.0`, pin then key.

[![Keystone Enabled](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-enabled-5cb9f8)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### 2. Payment Mandate, `mandate_ref` (authority)

What the agent may spend, bound to its passport.

Install: `pip install algovoi-payment-mandate-lite` or `npm i @algovoi/payment-mandate-lite`. Apache-2.0, pinned `0.1.0`, pin then key.

[![Keystone Enabled](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-enabled-5cb9f8)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### 3. Policy Binding, `policy_bound_ref` (policy in force)

Which policy snapshot the action runs under, version provable and rotation detectable.

Install: `pip install algovoi-policy-binding` or `npm i @algovoi/policy-binding`. Apache-2.0, pinned `0.1.0`, pin then key.

[![Keystone Enabled](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-enabled-5cb9f8)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### 4. Compliance Gate, `gate_ref` (compliance verdict)

The no-PII compliance verdict, bound to the policy it assessed.

Install: `pip install algovoi-compliance-gate-lite` or `npm i @algovoi/compliance-gate-lite`. Apache-2.0, pinned `0.1.0`, pin then key.

[![Keystone Enabled](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-enabled-5cb9f8)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### Compliance binding and decision basis (commercial)

The open Compliance Gate above emits the verdict. Substrate 2 binds that receipt into the keystone as a screen stage, proving the screening that informed this exact decision, and adds the signed decision basis: which compliance standards drove the verdict, the jurisdiction check bound to its geo determination, no PII and recomputable offline. Commercial only. Details: https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone

### 5. Spend Guardrail, `guardrail_ref` (pre-payment decision)

The ALLOW or DENY decision, bound to agent, mandate and policy.

Install: `pip install algovoi-spend-guardrail-lite` or `npm i @algovoi/spend-guardrail-lite`. Apache-2.0, pinned `0.1.0`, pin then key.

[![Keystone Enabled](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-enabled-5cb9f8)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### 6. Execution, `execution_ref` (decision-bound execution evidence)

What the agent actually did, bound to the exact decision that authorized it. `execution_ref` is the natural replacement for `action_ref`, the keystone-bound successor on the same JCS (RFC 8785) and SHA-256 discipline; `action_ref` stays fully backward compatible as the legacy primitive, unchanged in the substrate, so existing integrations keep verifying byte for byte with no forced migration. New work targets `execution_ref`; `action_ref` keeps working.

Install: `pip install algovoi-execution-ref` or `npm i @algovoi/execution-ref`. Apache-2.0, pinned `0.1.0`, pin then key.

[![Keystone Enabled](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-enabled-5cb9f8)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### 7. Cancellation, `cancellation_ref` (closes the authority)

Closes the mandate before execution, bound to the exact mandate.

Install: `pip install algovoi-cancellation-receipt-lite` or `npm i @algovoi/cancellation-receipt-lite`. Apache-2.0, pinned `0.1.0`, pin then key.

[![Keystone Enabled](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-enabled-5cb9f8)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### 8. Refund, `refund_ref` (after settlement)

A refund anchored to the execution that committed, not merely to the decision.

Install: `pip install algovoi-refund-receipt-lite` or `npm i @algovoi/refund-receipt-lite`. Apache-2.0, pinned `0.1.0`, pin then key.

[![Keystone Enabled](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-enabled-5cb9f8)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### 9. Composite Trust Query, `trust_query_ref` (one verdict over the chain)

One recomputable trust verdict over the ordered chain of references.

Install: `pip install algovoi-composite-trust-query-lite` or `npm i @algovoi/composite-trust-query-lite`. Apache-2.0, pinned `0.1.0`, pin then key.

[![Keystone Enabled](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-enabled-5cb9f8)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

Preconditions and transport, same pattern:

### Substrate Guard, `profile_ref` (input-bounds gate)

The input-bounds profile every record is admitted under before canonicalization.

Install: `pip install algovoi-substrate-guard` or `npm i @algovoi/substrate-guard`. Apache-2.0, pinned `0.1.0`, pin then key.

[![Keystone Enabled](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-enabled-5cb9f8)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### PEF Keystone (signed transport frames)

Wraps and pins a Keystone reference into hash-linked evidence frames.

Install: `pip install algovoi-pef-keystone` or `npm i @algovoi/pef-keystone`. Apache-2.0, pinned `0.1.0`, pin then key.

### TAP Verifier (offline receipt check)

Verifies an AlgoVoi TAP receipt with no AlgoVoi software: it re-derives the `receipt_id` from the JCS preimage and checks the Ed25519 signature using public libraries only, with an optional Falcon-1024 post-quantum check. For the Trusted Agent Protocol post-authentication audit trail.

Install: `pip install algovoi-tap-verifier` or `npm i @algovoi/tap-verifier`. Apache-2.0.

[![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### CloudEvents adapter (keystone decision as a CloudEvents 1.0 event)

Emits an AlgoVoi keystone decision as a CloudEvents 1.0 event; the content-addressed `execution_ref` is the event `id`, and a consumer recomputes it from the event `data` with JCS (RFC 8785) and SHA-256, with no AlgoVoi software.

Install: `pip install algovoi-cloudevents` or `npm i @algovoi/cloudevents`. Apache-2.0.

[![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### W3C Verifiable Credential adapter (keystone decision as a credential)

Emits an AlgoVoi keystone decision as a W3C Verifiable Credential (Data Model 2.0) of its own `KeystoneExecutionCredential` type; the content-addressed `execution_ref` is the `credentialSubject` id, recomputable from the subject before any signature suite is applied.

Install: `pip install algovoi-keystone-vc` or `npm i @algovoi/keystone-vc`. Apache-2.0.

[![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### MCP verifier (recompute a keystone execution_ref in any MCP client)

An open Model Context Protocol server exposing keystone verification as tools, so any MCP client recomputes and checks a keystone `execution_ref` offline, with no AlgoVoi service.

Install: `pip install algovoi-keystone-mcp` or `npm i @algovoi/keystone-mcp`. Apache-2.0.

[![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### Webhook verifier (verify a keystone ref in a webhook)

Verifies an AlgoVoi webhook HMAC signature and recomputes the keystone `execution_ref` carried in the event from its fields with JCS (RFC 8785) and SHA-256, so a consumer proves both the signature and that the keystone reference is authentic, with no AlgoVoi software.

Install: `pip install algovoi-webhook-verifier` or `npm i @algovoi/webhook-verifier`. Apache-2.0.

[![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### LangChain run trace (keystone decision on a LangChain run)

Attaches a keystone decision to a LangChain run as metadata and a tag under `algovoi.keystone.*`, so LangSmith or any tracer shows a content-addressed `execution_ref` a reviewer recomputes from the run alone, with no AlgoVoi software.

Install: `pip install algovoi-keystone-langchain` or `npm i @algovoi/keystone-langchain`. Apache-2.0.

[![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### CrewAI step trace (keystone decision on a CrewAI step)

Records a keystone decision once via a CrewAI step callback and passes the step output through unchanged, so a crew run carries a content-addressed `execution_ref` recomputable from the recorded metadata alone, with no AlgoVoi software.

Install: `pip install algovoi-keystone-crewai`. Apache-2.0.

[![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### AutoGen message trace (keystone decision on an AutoGen message)

Stamps a keystone decision into an AutoGen message metadata, so a conversation carries a content-addressed `execution_ref` recomputable from the message alone, with no AlgoVoi software.

Install: `pip install algovoi-keystone-autogen`. Apache-2.0.

[![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### ADK agent trace (keystone decision in Google ADK agent state)

Stamps a keystone decision into Google ADK agent state via a before-agent callback, so an agent run carries a content-addressed `execution_ref` recomputable from the state alone, with no AlgoVoi software.

Install: `pip install algovoi-keystone-adk`. Apache-2.0.

[![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### Orchestrator and composition proofs

The Keystone Orchestrator produces verifiable, end to end evidence that authority flowed correctly across organizational boundaries and was not exceeded, recomputable offline. The signed verdict is portable: it verifies off-the-shelf as a standard EdDSA JWS under any JOSE library and as a W3C Verifiable Credential under the Digital Bazaar eddsa-jcs-2022 suite, with no AlgoVoi software. Composition proofs are available on request. Docs: https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone

### Delegation: authority across parties (`delegation_ref`)

When authority is handed from one party to another, the Orchestrator proves it composed without anyone exceeding their grant. A treasury agent A, authorized for payments up to 1000 across GB and US, delegates a slice to a vendor agent B for a fixed window. B decides and executes deliberately narrower (a USDC transfer up to 500, GB). The Orchestrator composes A authority, the delegation, B decision and B execution into one signed verdict: authority flowed correctly across the A to B boundary and nothing was exceeded, verifiable offline. If B instead executes for 2000, the verdict is BROKEN: a signed receipt would still look valid, the composed proof does not.

The open `delegation_ref` is the tamper-evident binding for each hand-off. Install: `pip install algovoi-delegation-ref` or `npm i @algovoi/delegation-ref`. Apache-2.0, pinned `0.1.0`, pin then key. The cross-party scope-consistency proof is the Orchestrator capability; composition proofs available on request.

[![Keystone Enabled](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-enabled-5cb9f8)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### Revocation: pulling authority back (`revocation_ref`)

Authority can be withdrawn before it expires. When a grantor revokes a delegation, the Orchestrator proves that every downstream action which happened at or after the revocation no longer holds, even across several hops. A treasury agent A delegates to B, B sub-delegates to C, then A revokes the original grant. Any action C takes after that revocation composes to BROKEN, because C authority derived from a grant A had already pulled, recomputable offline. An action that happened before the revocation stays valid: revocation is prospective and provable from the bytes, not a mutable status flag. The open `revocation_ref` is available on request (Apache-2.0); the cross-party cascade proof is the commercial Orchestrator capability.

### Journey: the whole multi-agent task as one proof (`journey_ref`)

One reference binds an entire multi-agent task end to end: every hop execution and the delegations between them. Verifying a single `journey_ref` proves the whole A to B to C task at once: identity and authority continuity, scope never widened at any boundary, nothing acted under a revoked grant, and no hop omitted from the record. Drop a hop or widen scope anywhere and the journey composes to BROKEN. The open `journey_ref` is available on request (Apache-2.0); the end to end aggregation proof is the commercial Orchestrator capability.

### Journey adapters: bind the whole run in your framework (commercial)

The CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGen, and A2A journey adapters each record a multi-agent run hops and the delegations between them, then emit one `journey_ref` over the whole task: a crew, a graph, a group chat, or an agent-to-agent task verifies as a single proof.

Open A2A adapter: `pip install algovoi-a2a-journey`. Commercial full Orchestrator (delegation proofs plus PQC signing plus CCC): in the on-prem bundle.

[![Keystone Enabled](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-enabled-5cb9f8)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

### Internet-Drafts

Internet-Drafts for the underlying constructions (the canonicalization substrate, the receipt and execution references, and the audit chain of frames) are available on request.

### Benchmark, clean-box reproduction

Reproduced on a clean box, a fresh container with one vCPU, installing only from the public PyPI and npm registries:

- All 22 packages (11 PyPI, 11 npm) install and import on a clean box.
- Full conformance corpus v0.26.0: 31 vector sets plus every composition keystone reproduce byte for byte, Node equals Python.
- Single core soak, zero drift: 19,171 keystone recomputations per second on Python and 40,296 per second on Node, with zero drift across roughly 1.78 million recomputations.

---

## Substrate 2 (Commercial)

Everything above is open (Apache-2.0). Substrate 2 is the commercial core built on the same canonical evidence, with two simple parts.

**The control plane: where the pieces connect.** Think of it as the switchboard. Every service (payments, compliance, records, evidence) plugs into one hub that keeps the single list of trusted keys and issuers, lets each service register itself, and shows one live view of the whole system health.

**The keystone: the record of what actually happened.** A payment is checked for authorization, a decision is made, it executes, and it settles on chain. The keystone stitches those steps into one tamper-evident thread: each step is a short fingerprint locked to the one before it, so the whole story, from allowed to spend to settled, re-checks offline with no AlgoVoi software. The same record exports as a signed JSON receipt, a W3C Verifiable Credential, a JOSE token, or a zero-knowledge proof, each pointing back to the same payment.

The control plane connects the apps; the keystone is the thread that runs through a payment. Details: https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/substrate-2

### Keystone config panel

The keystone is an evolving ecosystem: each step has configurable parameters that shift as the platform grows. `algovoi-keystone-control` surfaces those parameters in a browser UI, auto-detects which algovoi packages are installed, and lets operators edit them via a pin-gated HTTPS panel. Open (Apache-2.0).

Install: `pip install algovoi-keystone-control`. Docs: https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone

### Keystone connectors

Drop-in adapters that bind a data-layer operation to the keystone decision that authorised it, emitting a content-addressed `execution_ref` (verifiable offline with `keystone-verify`). Open Apache-2.0, available on request:

- `algovoi-keystone-odbc`: wraps any ODBC / DB-API cursor; every execute (insert / update / delete) is bound to its `decision_ref`, so a write can be proven consistent with the decision that allowed it.

  [![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

- `algovoi-keystone-sqlalchemy`: one `bind_session()` call registers an `after_flush` listener; each flushed ORM change is bound to the keystone, no model or query changes.

  [![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

- `algovoi-keystone-kafka`: wraps any producer (kafka-python / confluent-kafka / aiokafka); each produced message carries an `execution_ref`, with failed sends recorded as `FAILED`.

  [![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

- `algovoi-keystone-openlineage`: attaches a keystone run facet to each OpenLineage RunEvent, so the lineage standard own events carry the `execution_ref`; outcome derived from `eventType`.

  [![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

- `algovoi-keystone-asgi`: one ASGI / WSGI middleware (FastAPI / Starlette / Flask / Django) binds every state-changing HTTP request to its `decision_ref`; outcome from the response status.

  [![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

- `algovoi-keystone-grpc`: a gRPC server interceptor binds each unary call to its `decision_ref`; outcome COMMITTED, or FAILED if the handler raises. Streaming passes through.

  [![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

- `algovoi-keystone-s3`: wraps any boto3 S3 client so every object write (put / delete) carries an `execution_ref` keyed to `bucket/key`; reads pass through untouched.

  [![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

- `algovoi-keystone-redis`: wraps any redis-py client so every write command (set / delete / hset / expire) carries an `execution_ref` keyed to the key; reads pass through.

  [![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

- `algovoi-keystone-mongo`: wraps any pymongo collection so every write (insert / update / delete / replace) carries an `execution_ref` keyed to `db.collection`; reads pass through.

  [![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

- `algovoi-keystone-elasticsearch`: wraps any elasticsearch-py client so every write (index / update / delete / bulk) carries an `execution_ref` keyed to `index/doc_id`; searches pass through.

  [![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

- `algovoi-keystone-nats`: wraps any nats-py connection so every publish carries an `execution_ref` keyed to the subject; subscribes and requests pass through.

  [![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)

- `algovoi-keystone-gcs`: wraps any Google Cloud Storage blob so every object write (upload / delete) carries an `execution_ref` keyed to `bucket/name`; reads pass through.

  [![Keystone Integration](https://img.shields.io/badge/Keystone-integration-7c8aa0)](https://docs.algovoi.co.uk/keystone)
